title: The Will of Ashcombe
premise: When archivist Tamsin Brightwater receives a confession letter postmarked the day after old Lady Ashcombe's funeral, they learn the town's beloved matriarch did not die of natural causes—and that the letter's writer expects to be dead before anyone reads it. Digging through twelve years of cathedral records, Tamsin uncovers a pattern of quiet deaths the town filed away as misfortune, all tied to the locked crypt beneath St. Aldhelm's. As Tamsin closes in on the truth, they discover their own found family—the verger, the florist, the retired sexton—each harboring pieces of the secret, and one of them holding the key to the crypt and the poison. In the end, Tamsin must choose between exposing the killer they've come to love or letting Ashcombe's last secret stay buried, choosing instead to open the crypt, publish the truth, and finally claim a name and place of their own.
about_author: Hazel Oyelaran is a former parish records volunteer who spent years cataloguing centuries of small-town paperwork and the silences between it. She writes mysteries about people who keep archives—and the pasts that refuse to stay archived.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. We meet Tamsin in the cathedral archive, cataloguing condolence cards after Lady Ashcombe's funeral, establishing their careful invisibility and warm but guarded ties to the verger Edith and sexton Bram. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as order.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A confession letter arrives claiming Lady Ashcombe was murdered, postmarked the day after her funeral—but unsigned except for an initial: V. The doctor certified heart failure. Tamsin hides the letter, then can't stop reading it. Beat: dread cracking routine.

chapters.title: What the Doctor Ordered
chapters.summary: Dr. Pellowe's POV. The town physician deflects Tamsin's questions with practiced ease, revealing he signed the certificate without an autopsy at the family's request. He mentions a second death years ago he also waved through. Beat: complicity wearing respectability.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Misfortune
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Searching the archive's death registers, Tamsin finds four deaths in twelve years—all 'heart failure,' all connected to Ashcombe House staff. Someone has been tidying the record long before Tamsin arrived. Beat: the archive itself becomes evidence.

chapters.title: The Verger's Silence
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith warns Tamsin to stop asking questions, revealing she saw someone leaving the crypt the night of the funeral. Her loyalty to the cathedral wars with what she knows. Beat: fear dressed as piety.

chapters.title: Locked Below
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The sexton admits only three keys exist for the crypt: his, the late Lady Ashcombe's, and one unaccounted for since 2013—the year of the first suspicious death. Beat: guilt surfacing like groundwater.

chapters.title: The Nephew Returns
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Sir Marcus Ashcombe arrives to settle the estate, charming and impatient, pushing to seal the crypt permanently and donate its contents to a London auction house. Tamsin stalls him using archival regulations. Beat: class friction and first real danger.

chapters.title: A Letter from V
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Handwriting analysis against old parish correspondence points to Vivian Marsh, the florist who supplied Ashcombe House for decades—and Tamsin's closest friend. Beat: betrayal blooming where trust grew.

chapters.title: Flowers for the Dead
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. Vivian recalls delivering foxglove-laced arrangements to the house for years, insisting she never knew what they were for—until she did. She confesses she wrote the letter but swears she isn't the killer. Beat: terror wrapped in tenderness.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Reviewing the estate inventory, Tamsin finds Lady Ashcombe's own journal listed among items bound for London—a journal whose final pages are missing. Marcus wants it gone. Beat: the race narrows.

chapters.title: What the Journal Said
chapters.summary: Recovered journal pages, Lady Ashcombe's voice. She documented blackmail within her household: someone poisoning slowly, extorting her silence about a decades-old scandal involving a child given away. Beat: the victim becomes narrator.

chapters.title: The Child Who Left
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Parish baptismal records reveal the scandal: a baby born at Ashcombe House in 1989 and quietly placed for adoption—records Tamsin personally processed on arrival twelve years ago. The realization lands: the cover-up runs through Tamsin's own hands. Beat: identity shaken.

chapters.title: Threats in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Someone ransacks the archive overnight; the confession letter and register pages vanish. Edith finds Tasmkin's office door scratched with a warning: SOME CASES STAY CLOSED. Beat: isolation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Marcus's Version
chapters.summary: Sir Marcus's POV. Under pressure, Marcus reveals he knew about the blackmail payments and suspected the killer was protecting the family name—including his own illegitimate half-sibling's existence. He denies murder but admits paying the blackmailer after his aunt's death. Beat: motive multiplying.

chapters.title: The Third Key
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram confesses he gave the third key years ago to Dr. Pellowe—for 'emergencies'—and has suspected since the first death. His silence bought his cottage and his grandchild's school fees. Beat: ordinary corruption, extraordinary cost.

chapters.title: Exhumation
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Armed with the journal pages, Tamsin forces a police review; Lady Ashcombe is exhumed and digitalis poisoning confirmed. But the detective notes the poisoner needed medical knowledge. All eyes turn to Pellowe. Beat: vindication shadowed by doubt.

chapters.title: Pellowe's Confession
chapters.summary: Dr. Pellowe's POV. Cornered, Pellowe admits to the deaths—but claims he acted as Lady Ashcombe's instrument, mercy-killing the blackmailer's victims at her written instruction, until she decided to end it herself and he helped. The letter, he says, was meant for someone else. Beat: moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Who Was V?
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Re-examining the letter's paper and ink, Tamsin realizes it matches cathedral stationery from the vestry—written by someone with access the night of the funeral. Not Vivian. Edith. Beat: the ground gives way beneath found family.

chapters.title: Edith's Truth
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith confesses she is the child born at Ashcombe House in 1989, raised unknowingly by the woman who gave her up, and that she confronted Lady Ashcombe the night she died—not to kill, but the confrontation triggered the fatal dose already in her system. She wrote the letter expecting to hang for it. Beat: grief and love colliding.

chapters.title: The Crypt Opens
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. At the hearing, Tamsin testifies that the evidence shows no intent to kill—only a lifetime of secrets killing everyone they touched. Edith walks free; Marcus withdraws the auction; the crypt is opened and its records made public. Beat: light entering a sealed room.

chapters.title: Ashes, Filed Properly
chapters.summary: Vivian and Tamsin's shared POV. The town absorbs the truth unevenly; some doors close to Tamsin forever. Vivian and Tamsin rebuild their friendship honestly, and Edith returns to the verger's path with the town's grudging blessing. Beat: forgiveness as slow work.

chapters.title: A Name of One's Own
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin installs a public exhibit in the opened crypt—every name, every date, nothing alphabetized away—and adds their own entry to the parish roll for the first time: not just the archivist, but a person of Ashcombe. Final beat: invisibility surrendered, belonging claimed.
